title: Does Hindman’s theorem imply the ω-jump?
formal: Over RCA₀, does Hindman’s finite-sums theorem imply ACA₀⁺? Equivalently, does RCA₀+HT prove that every set X has an ω-th Turing jump?
definitions: Work in classical two-sorted second-order arithmetic, with number variables and variables for sets of natural numbers. RCA₀ has the usual elementary arithmetic axioms, Σ⁰₁ induction and Δ⁰₁ comprehension, allowing set parameters. HT is the assertion that for every integer k≥1 and every coloring c of the positive integers into {0,…,k−1}, there exist an infinite set H of positive integers and a color i such that c(Σ_{h∈F}h)=i for every nonempty finite subset F of H. Terms in a sum are distinct; there is no fixed upper bound on their number and no additional sparsity requirement on H. For a set X, its Turing jump X′ is {e: the e-th oracle Turing machine with oracle X halts on input e}, using one fixed effective enumeration. The ω-jump existence axiom says ∀X∃Y [Y₀=X and ∀j(Y_{j+1}=Y_j′)], where Y_j={e:⟨j,e⟩∈Y} and ⟨·,·⟩ is a fixed primitive recursive pairing. ACA₀⁺ is RCA₀ plus that axiom. The question is formal provability of this implication over the stated base, not truth of Hindman’s theorem in ordinary set theory and not a single-instance computability claim.
answer_criterion: Prove the ω-jump existence axiom in RCA₀+HT, or prove nonimplication by constructing a model of RCA₀+HT in which some set has no coded ω-jump. A standard-natural-number model is sufficient for a separation but is not required. A lower bound of ACA₀ alone, an upper bound of ACA₀⁺, or a theorem about only bounded-length sums does not decide this implication. A negative answer need not show that HT is equivalent to ACA₀; an intermediate strength would also refute the implication.
context:
Hindman’s theorem says that a finite coloring contains an infinite set whose entire collection of finite sums has one color. This is much more than finding an infinite monochromatic subset: the same color must work for single elements, pairs, triples and every larger finite selection. For parity coloring, the positive even numbers give an immediate example. The theorem must also handle colorings with no such simple arithmetic description.

The combinatorial statement is a theorem, not the unresolved claim on this card. Reverse mathematics asks which set-existence axioms are needed to prove it. One works over a deliberately weak base theory and compares stronger principles by implication. The inherited paper records the classical bounds ACA₀⁺⇒HT⇒ACA₀ and identifies closing this gap as a major open problem. This card asks specifically whether the upper implication reverses.

ACA₀ allows arithmetic comprehension; equivalently over the base theory, every set has its Turing jump. An individual jump supplies answers to halting questions relative to the given set. Repeating that operation a fixed finite number of times yields increasingly strong information. The ω-jump places every finite iterate into the sections of one set. Being able to discuss each fixed finite stage is not the same as having this whole sequence available as a single object.

The distinction is visible in the model consisting of the standard natural numbers together with all arithmetical sets. It is closed under the ordinary Turing jump, since jumping an arithmetical set still yields an arithmetical set. It does not contain the join of all finite jumps of the empty set. Thus ACA₀⁺ demands more set existence than ACA₀. Whether Hindman’s theorem already forces that additional existence is the precise issue here.

The computability bounds show why ordinary computable colorings already matter. The account by Csima and coauthors recalls a computable coloring for which every finite-sums solution computes the halting set, and an upper bound placing a solution in the (ω+1)-st jump of the coloring. These are bounds on information in solutions. Neither identifies the exact reverse-mathematical strength, and noncomputability alone falls far short of an ω-jump reversal.

Restricted sum lengths have provided substantial progress without closing the full gap. Carlucci–Kołodziejczyk–Lepore–Zdanowski prove that the version requiring monochromatic singletons and pairs already implies ACA₀; four colors suffice without an additional sparsity condition. Their results for sums of exactly n≥3 terms use an apartness condition on the binary supports of the chosen integers. These carefully specified variants should not be merged with unrestricted HT.

Even replacing “at most two” by “exactly two” changes the logical picture. Csima and coauthors construct a computable two-color instance of the exactly-two version with no Σ⁰₂ solution and prove a lower bound through diagonally noncomputable functions relative to the halting set. Yet exactly-two sums follow from Ramsey’s theorem for pairs, placing that principle strictly below full HT over the base. This is a useful warning that small wording changes can alter the problem.

There is a separate combinatorial principle known to capture the desired upper level exactly. Carlucci–Zdanowski prove that Ramsey’s theorem for exactly large finite sets is equivalent to ACA₀⁺. A finite set F is exactly large when |F|=min(F)+1, so its dimension varies with its elements. This yields a potential comparison target: an implication from HT to this precisely defined Ramsey principle would suffice. Its equivalence does not itself supply that missing implication.

Recent results in the neighboring theory of variable words require the same care. Liu–Patey’s June 2026 preprint, revised in July, gives low₂ solutions to the Ordered Variable Word theorem for colorings of ordinary words and proves each fixed-dimensional unordered Carlson–Simpson lemma in ACA₀. The paper distinguishes these principles from ordered higher-dimensional counterparts and still describes ACA₀⁺ as the weakest known system proving HT. Its new upper bounds should not be transferred to Hindman’s theorem.

Le Houérou–Patey’s July 2026 preprint obtains a conservation result for a one-variable Carlson–Simpson principle with two colors. It controls which arithmetical consequences that particular principle adds to a weak theory. This is a different assertion from constructing the ω-jump out of unrestricted finite-sums homogeneity. Together the recent papers sharpen nearby boundaries without answering the implication stated here.

A positive answer would make a concrete additive-combinatorial theorem a characterization of closure under all finite Turing jumps at once. A negative answer would show that known proofs use more set existence than the theorem itself entails. Either outcome would clarify the information content of an infinite combinatorial search principle, which is the reason for its place in the computability part of this catalogue.
why: A longstanding gap in the computational and axiomatic strength of a central infinite combinatorial theorem, with a precise target at the ω-th Turing jump.

importance.reason: A landmark reverse-mathematical calibration problem connecting finite-sums combinatorics, oracle computation and the hierarchy of set-existence axioms.

progress.text: Blass–Hirst–Simpson establish ACA₀⁺⇒HT⇒ACA₀ over RCA₀, leaving the reversal in this card open.
Carlucci–Zdanowski characterize ACA₀⁺ using Ramsey’s theorem for exactly large sets; this supplies a comparison principle rather than an HT reversal.
Carlucci–Kołodziejczyk–Lepore–Zdanowski reach the ACA₀ lower bound already for sums of at most two elements with four colors; conference precursor 2017, journal version 2020.
Csima and coauthors prove nontrivial computability and reverse-mathematical lower bounds for sums of exactly two elements, a weaker principle than full HT.
Liu–Patey prove new upper bounds and separations for variable-word and unordered Carlson–Simpson principles, without claiming a resolution of HT’s strength.
Le Houérou–Patey obtain a conservation theorem for a one-variable, two-color Carlson–Simpson principle.

status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No proof or separation for RCA₀+HT⇒ACA₀⁺ was found in the checked primary literature. The recent variable-word and Carlson–Simpson results have different formulations and do not establish this reversal.
